Empirical Research Plan: Schooling and Adult Mortality, U.S. Birth Cohorts 1914-1939
=========================================================================

1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------
Strategy: Two–sample, two-stage least squares (2SLS) / difference-in-differences–style instrumental variables.  

• First stage: use changes in state-level compulsory‐attendance and child-labor statutes (Entry-Age, Work-Permit-Age, Continuation-School requirements) that hit different birth-state × birth-cohort cells at different times to predict completed years of schooling.  
• Second stage: regress 10-year age–specific mortality rates on the predicted schooling.  
Why appropriate?  
a. Policy changes are plausibly exogenous to any one cohort’s latent health endowment.  
b. Laws were enforced during 1920-40, giving a strong first-stage.  
c. The design controls flexibly for birth-state fixed effects and cohort fixed effects, so identification comes from within-state changes over time (a DID flavor).  
d. Mortality is measured after schooling is complete, so reverse causality is ruled out.

2. Treatment and Control
------------------------
Treatment variable (endogenous):  
• EDU_scg = mean completed years of schooling of whites born in state s, cohort c, gender g.

Instruments (policy “treatments”):  
• EntryAge_sc = minimum legal age at school entry.  
• WorkAge_sc = minimum age for full-time work permit (higher ⇒ longer time in school).  
• ContSchool_sc = indicator that minors with work permits must attend continuation school part-time.  

Control (counterfactual): cohorts in the same state born before a legal change and cohorts in other states where the law did not change.  

Treatment timing: the law is coded as “in force” for cohorts who turned 14 on or after 1 July of the calendar year the statute became effective (observed at age 14 because that is our aggregation age).

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------
A1. Relevance: Statutory changes increased (or decreased) average schooling.  
Plausibility: Compulsory-school studies for this era show 0.2–0.4 additional grades per year of mandated attendance.

A2. Exclusion (Independence): The schooling laws affect adult mortality only through the schooling margin, not via concurrent health programs.  
Plausibility: These laws were education-specific; school-lunch, public-health insurance, etc. did not yet exist or were federal-level and common across states.

A3. Parallel Trends / No state-specific shocks correlated with policy: In absence of the law change, treated and untreated cohorts would have followed parallel mortality trends within state.  
Plausibility: We include state×linear-cohort trends and the rich set of state-at-14 controls to absorb differential trends.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no interstate spillovers): One state’s law does not change mortality of cohorts born in another state.  
Plausibility: Schooling statutes applied only to residents; cross-state commuting of 6-15-year-olds was negligible.

A5. Monotonicity: Raising compulsory attendance cannot reduce schooling for anyone (no “defiers”).  
Plausibility: Reasonable—minimum schooling years only increase or leave unchanged each child’s completed years.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
-----------------------------------------
T1. Selective Migration: Families could move to evade stringent laws; by adult age people live elsewhere, so mortality is measured where they die, not where they were schooled.  
Mitigation: Use state of birth rather than state of residence for both schooling and mortality denominators; show that net migration rates of 14-year-olds are uncorrelated with law changes.

T2. Laws coincide with other state reforms (e.g., public-health spending) that directly influence mortality.  
Mitigation: Control for state-level contemporaneous covariates (doctors per capita, per-capita health expenditures, manufacturing wages, urbanization) interacted with cohort polynomials; run placebo tests on cohorts aged 25-34 during law change who should be unaffected educationally.

T3. Measurement error in mortality rates constructed from Census counts.  
Mitigation: a) show consistency with NHEFS micro survival data; b) weight cells by inverse of sampling variance; c) replicate using only large-population cells.

5. R Code Outline
-----------------
```r
############################################################
# 0. Packages
############################################################
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast FELM / IV
library(ivreg)       # alternative
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

############################################################
# 1. Load and merge data
############################################################
cells  <- fread("ipums_aggregated_cells.csv")   # state*cohort*gender cells
laws   <- fread("compulsory_schooling_laws.csv")# state*year law matrix

# Merge statutory variables to cells by state and cohort (age 14 criterion)
cells[, year14 := birth_year + 14]
cells <- merge(cells,
               laws, 
               by.x = c("state", "year14"), 
               by.y = c("state", "year"),
               all.x = TRUE)

############################################################
# 2. Variable construction
############################################################
# 10-year mortality rate per 1,000
cells[, mort_6070 := deaths_60_70 / population_1960 * 1000]
cells[, mort_7080 := deaths_70_80 / population_1970 * 1000]

# Stack the two decades
mort <- melt(cells,
             id.vars = c("state","birth_year","gender","edu_mean",
                         "EntryAge","WorkAge","ContSchool",
                         "controls..."),
             measure.vars = patterns("^mort_"),
             variable.name = "mort_window",
             value.name   = "mort_rate")

# First-stage instrument: years of compulsory schooling implied by laws
mort[, comp_years := pmax(0, WorkAge - EntryAge)] # simple example

# Sample weight (inverse variance of a proportion)
mort[, weight := population_1960]   # rough; refine if desired

############################################################
# 3. Main 2SLS specification
############################################################
# FE: state and cohort
fe_formula <- "~ state + birth_year"

iv_formula <- as.formula(
  "mort_rate ~ edu_mean | . -edu_mean + comp_years | 0 | state"
)

# Using fixest
iv_mod <- feols(iv_formula,
                data   = mort,
                fixef  = ~ state + birth_year,
                weights = ~ weight,
                cluster = ~ state)

summary(iv_mod)

############################################################
# 4. Robustness: add state×cohort linear trend
############################################################
mort[, cohort_center := birth_year - 1926]     # center at mid-point
rob_formula <- as.formula(
  "mort_rate ~ edu_mean + state:cohort_center | . -edu_mean + comp_years | 0 | state"
)

iv_mod2 <- feols(rob_formula,
                 data = mort,
                 fixef = ~ state + birth_year,
                 weights = ~ weight,
                 cluster = ~ state)

etable(list(Main = iv_mod, Trend = iv_mod2))
```

6. Expected Results
-------------------
Economic theory (Grossman model) predicts that additional schooling raises the efficiency of health production and increases the present value of future life, so mortality should fall. Prior empirical IV estimates from similar contexts (U.S. 1920s schooling laws) suggest −2 to −3 deaths per 1,000 over a 10-year window per extra year of schooling. I expect a negative coefficient roughly in that range (≈ −0.25 pp on a 1-percent-scale 10-year mortality).

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)
------------------------------------------------
C1: Strong first stage (F-stat > 10) – 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction credible – 0.7  
C3: No simultaneous policy shocks – 0.6  
C4: No selective migration bias – 0.8  
C5: Homogeneous LATE interpretation clear – 0.9  

(Overall ≈ 4.0 / 5)
